subject.role: Anchorage Assembly Member, District 1 (North Anchorage), Seat B
subject.anchorage_tie: Elected April 2026 to represent District 1 (North/downtown Anchorage), replacing Christopher Constant; bowl-based elected official whose ordinance directly governs APD surveillance operating inside the Anchorage bowl.

subject_quotes.verbatim: We want to do things right. Let's put this into code now, so that when power changes, when the political winds shift, as they always do, we have protections for the people, no matter who is overseeing and implementing the system.
subject_quotes.context: Explaining why she is co-sponsoring the surveillance-restriction ordinance ahead of the APD Real-Time Crime Center expansion

subject_quotes.verbatim: We need to increase trust before we increase the power of this surveillance system.
subject_quotes.context: On sequencing privacy guardrails before expanding the crime center's camera/AI capabilities

decision.what_happened: Ordinance AO 2026-108, co-sponsored by Scout, aims at clarifying 'existing restrictions on surveillance technology' and 'establishing new restrictions on license plate reader systems, real-time crime center operations, and live camera monitoring.' Per multiple outlets, the ordinance would prevent the police department from adding artificial intelligence technology with human-feature recognition capabilities into the network without Assembly approval (subject to a period of 'temporary approval' and annual reporting), require a case number for each surveillance data search, require the city to erase individuals' data after two weeks unless used as evidence in an active investigation, and prohibit sharing footage with out-of-state or federal agencies without a warrant.
decision.the_binary: Sponsor binding municipal code requiring prior Assembly approval before APD can deploy AI human-feature/facial recognition (plus 2-week data retention and warrant limits) versus letting the RTCC's ~750-camera/ALPR network and any future AI recognition tooling be adopted at executive/APD discretion with no legislative guardrails.
decision.ak_consequence: Public-safety technology + AI-governance policy. Codifies who authorizes algorithmic facial/human-feature recognition on the Municipality of Anchorage's Real-Time Crime Center (up to ~750 cameras, 250+ traffic cams, drones, ALPR). Affected actors: APD, MOA residents, AI-surveillance vendors. Timeframe: public hearing Sept 1, 2026, landing before/alongside the pending ~$600k RTCC expansion and the 2027 budget cycle.
decision.prelim_debatable_axis: Sharp read: gets ahead of AI facial recognition before deployment, codifies civil-liberties guardrails and a vendor-neutral AI-approval process, builds cross-ideological trust. Weak read: adds Assembly-approval friction to legitimate crime-fighting, a two-week retention cap could impede investigations, and it partly duplicates the Assembly's 2023 facial-recognition ban, arguably a symbolic layer atop a procurement fight rather than durable AI policy.

candidate_subjects.recurrence_note: AO 2026-108 is co-sponsored with Keith McCormick (HARD-BLOCKED this cycle, profiled 2026-08-14) and Vice Chair Daniel Volland. It is the policy counterpart to the blocked Thundercat/RTCC procurement cluster but is a DISTINCT new ordinance (AI/surveillance governance code), not the Thundercat contract vote. Scout has never been profiled by this desk.
candidate_subjects.orchestrator_caveat: Scout could not retrieve the Legistar/muni.org AO 2026-108 ordinance PDF (guessed URL 404'd). VALIDATOR MUST attempt to pull the AO 2026-108 record and the Sept 1 agenda packet from meetings.muni.org or anchorageak.legistar.com as the true primary source. If the municipal record is unreachable, judge whether four independent news outlets carrying the ordinance number, sponsors, and provisions is sufficient corroboration to ship caveated.

subject.role: Anchorage Assembly Vice Chair, District 1 (Downtown/North Anchorage)
subject.anchorage_tie: Sitting Assembly Vice Chair representing District 1 in the Anchorage bowl; co-sponsor of the ordinance governing APD surveillance/AI inside the municipality.

decision.what_happened: Ordinance AO 2026-108, co-sponsored by Vice Chair Volland, would set new restrictions on automatic license plate readers, real-time crime center operations, and live camera monitoring, and would prevent the police department from adding artificial intelligence technology with human-feature recognition capabilities into the network without Assembly approval, alongside a two-week data-retention limit and a warrant requirement before sharing footage with out-of-state or federal agencies.
decision.the_binary: Co-sponsor codified Assembly pre-approval for AI human-feature recognition on the RTCC versus deferring to the administration on if/when AI surveillance tooling is added.
decision.ak_consequence: Same as the Scout candidate. Establishes municipal AI-surveillance governance over APD's RTCC before facial/human-feature recognition is deployed; public hearing Sept 1, 2026.
decision.prelim_debatable_axis: As vice chair, Volland lends institutional weight to codifying AI guardrails, but no verbatim quote from Volland on this decision was found in fetched sources, so his individual ownership is weaker than Scout's.

candidate_subjects.recurrence_note: Same ordinance as the Scout candidate. Offered as an alternate named owner. Weaker because no fetched primary source captured a Volland quote specific to this ordinance.

subject.role: Executive Vice President and Chief Information Officer
subject.anchorage_tie: Northrim Bank is headquartered in Anchorage (a ~$3.4B Alaska-based bank); Reed is its Anchorage-based EVP/CIO. The platform decision governs digital banking for Northrim customers statewide plus the Pacific Northwest.

subject_quotes.verbatim: Our customers increasingly expect a seamless, intuitive digital experience regardless of where they live. With Narmi, we're investing in technology that allows us to deliver the convenience customers expect while maintaining the local service and personal relationships that set Northrim apart. Narmi's transparency, expertise in FIS IBS, and willingness to go above and beyond made them the right choice to power this transformation.
subject_quotes.context: Reed explaining Northrim's selection of the Narmi One platform in the launch press release

decision.what_happened: Northrim Bank selected the Narmi One platform (Narmi is described in the release as 'a leader in AI-powered digital banking') to modernize its digital banking ecosystem, unifying digital banking and account opening for customers across Alaska and the Pacific Northwest.
decision.the_binary: Reed chose the New York fintech Narmi's AI-powered One platform to run Northrim's digital front door over building/keeping an in-house or incumbent stack. He could have picked a competing vendor or deferred modernization.
decision.ak_consequence: Financial services / fintech. A ~$3.4B Anchorage-headquartered community bank outsources its customer-facing digital-banking and account-opening experience to an out-of-state AI-powered platform, affecting Northrim retail and business customers across Alaska and the Pacific Northwest through a multi-quarter migration. Northrim is simultaneously hiring an RPA & AI Systems Engineer, signaling internal automation buildout.
decision.prelim_debatable_axis: Sharp read: a modern AI-powered digital front door lets a small Alaska bank compete with national banks in a state where geography makes branches impractical. Critical read: a community bank hands its customer-facing digital core and customer data to a Lower-48 fintech, raising vendor lock-in, data-governance and cost questions, and 'AI-powered' may be more marketing than substance for a banking-services swap.

candidate_subjects.recurrence_note: Covered by Alaska Business Magazine, Finextra, Yahoo Finance, and Morningstar/AccessWire, but ALL coverage traces to the single Narmi/Northrim press release, so it is effectively SINGLE-SOURCED. Validator must weigh this against the multi-source corroboration gate.
candidate_subjects.orchestrator_caveat: AI nexus is the weakest of the pool. 'AI-powered digital banking' is the vendor's own marketing framing in a press release; the decision object is a digital-banking platform swap, not an AI deployment per se.

subject.org: Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority (AIDEA)
subject.anchorage_tie: AIDEA is the state's development finance authority headquartered in Anchorage; Ruaro is its Anchorage-based executive director. The proposed data-center-ready industrial park sits roughly 60 road miles north of Anchorage in the Mat-Su and would draw on Railbelt utility corridors that also serve the Anchorage bowl.

subject_quotes.verbatim: there are no pre-determined and set land use decisions made by AIDEA
subject_quotes.context: Ruaro, in a statement to Alaska's News Source, responding to concerns that AIDEA had already committed the parcel to data centers; he said land-use decisions would follow the land transfer and local consultation

decision.what_happened: AIDEA is pursuing a noncompetitive purchase from the Alaska Department of Natural Resources of roughly 30-31 square miles of state land north of Houston for a 'multi-use industrial and energy development district' whose stated components include a freight/logistics hub, utility transmission corridors, advanced manufacturing pads, and 'development of scalable data centers that leverage existing and planned utility corridors.' DNR released a preliminary decision on the noncompetitive sale in mid/late July 2026, with public comment open through August 19, 2026.
decision.the_binary: Ruaro/AIDEA chose to file for and advance a noncompetitive (sole-source) DNR land acquisition of ~30 sq mi expressly to create data-center- and large-load-ready industrial land, rather than not pursue the land, pursue a smaller footprint, or route it through a competitive land process.
decision.ak_consequence: Energy/land/AI-infrastructure siting. A state authority is assembling compute-ready industrial land in the Mat-Su tied to Railbelt utility corridors on a grid where Chugach and other utilities have publicly said they currently cannot power a large AI data center amid the Cook Inlet gas shortfall. Local Houston/Mat-Su residents face wildlife-habitat and recreation-access tradeoffs. DNR comment closed Aug 19, 2026, with a Finding and Final Decision to follow later in 2026.
decision.prelim_debatable_axis: Sharp read: Alaska has only 8 data centers (fourth-fewest nationally); proactively banking utility-served industrial land could capture AI-infrastructure investment before demand materializes. Weak read: a noncompetitive 30-sq-mi land transfer for 'scalable data centers' is speculative given a gas-constrained Railbelt that utilities say cannot power large loads, concentrates land in one authority without competition, and imposes concrete environmental costs for uncertain payoff. Ruaro's 'no pre-determined land use' framing sits awkwardly against an application that explicitly names data centers.

candidate_subjects.recurrence_note: AIDEA's underlying application was filed in December (OUT of the 60-day window); the in-window artifact is the DNR preliminary decision and comment period, which is AGENCY-owned rather than Ruaro-owned. Distinct from the blocked Sparrow Mahoney/STAK North Slope DNR lease (different org, land, decision).
candidate_subjects.orchestrator_caveat: Two soft spots for the validator to judge: (1) Anchorage tie is institutional (AIDEA HQ) rather than geographic (land is in Mat-Su); (2) the in-window artifact is DNR's action, not Ruaro's, so decision ownership may fail the gate.

subject.role: Professor of Biological Sciences (geomicrobiology/applied microbiology); Director, Advanced Instrumentation in Microbiome Sciences (AIMS)
subject.org: University of Alaska Anchorage (UAA), Department of Biological Sciences
subject.anchorage_tie: UAA is in the Anchorage bowl; Briggs is a UAA-based professor whose lab (AIMS) and glacier-microbe rare-earth work are run out of Anchorage. UAA is the LEAD institution on the NSF EPSCoR award.

decision.what_happened: NSF FY2026 EPSCoR award (Focused EPSCoR Collaboration): 'Transformative Bioprocessing and AI-Driven Frameworks for Sustainable Critical Mineral Recovery'. 'The project establishes a Smart Bio-Refinery framework with AI-enabled microbial recovery systems to address the nation's reliance on foreign sources of rare earth elements.' Participating institutions: University of Alaska Anchorage (listed first / lead), Montana Technological University, University of Alaska Fairbanks, University of Wyoming (subawardee). UAA award ID 2614749; UAF award ID 2614751.
decision.the_binary: Pursuing an AI-enabled biological (microbial 'Smart Bio-Refinery') route to rare-earth recovery as the Anchorage-led node of a four-institution collaboration versus a conventional non-AI processing approach or letting UAF lead.
decision.ak_consequence: Critical minerals / mining plus university research capacity. Share of the FY2026 EPSCoR cohort ($39.9M across 8 awards; individual UAA/UAF amounts not disclosed). Multi-year, starting FY2026.
decision.prelim_debatable_axis: Sharp: puts an Anchorage lab at the head of a national-security-relevant AI-plus-bioprocessing critical-minerals effort. Questionable: thematically overlaps the already-funded UAF-led NSF Critical Mineral Accelerator Engine (Munk, blocked pair), and 'AI-driven' framing in an EPSCoR abstract can outrun near-term AI deliverables.

candidate_subjects.recurrence_note: Distinct from the blocked Lee Ann Munk / NSF Critical Mineral Accelerator Engine pair (different award, different lead institution, different mechanism).
candidate_subjects.orchestrator_caveat: CRITICAL: the scout could NOT locate any primary source naming Briggs as PI on award 2614749. NSF's award record is not yet populated and UAA has issued no release. His PI role is INFERRED. Unless the validator confirms the named PI from a primary source, this candidate FAILS the named-subject gate and must be dropped, not softened.
